title: This portfolio
tagline: Designed, built and tested by me — no framework
summary: The site you are reading. I designed it in Figma and built it as a static site with its own generator: one JSON file per project, a Python script that writes every page, and a test suite that runs against the generated HTML. Built end to end with an AI-assisted workflow, which is how I work now — the fastest way I know to find out whether an interaction actually holds up is to build it.
description: A static portfolio site designed and built end to end — JSON content, a Python generator, an image pipeline and a test suite, with no framework and no runtime dependencies.
team: One — me, with an AI-assisted workflow
status: Live — you are looking at it

sections.heading: The site
sections.body:
Dark-only and declared as such, so the browser paints scrollbars and form controls to match rather than guessing. Every colour, type step and spacing value comes from a single tokens file; the stylesheet contains no literals, so changing the accent is a one-line edit.

It is built progressive-enhancement first. The marquee, the lightbox and the scroll reveals are all additions — with JavaScript switched off the site still renders completely, which is also how these screenshots were taken.

images.alt: The portfolio homepage rendered on a phone-width viewport
images.caption: Same content column at every breakpoint. The two work tiers collapse from three-up to one.

sections.heading: The system
sections.body: The JSON is read at build time, not in the browser. fetch() is blocked on file://, so a site that loaded its own content at runtime would break the moment someone double-clicked index.html — baking it in keeps the site working from the filesystem and from a server.

images.alt: A project's content.json next to the HTML that build.py generates from it
images.caption: One JSON file per project, and 1,085 lines of Python that write every page. No page is ever hand-edited.

sections.heading: The guardrail
sections.body: The tests assert against the real generated HTML rather than the source JSON, because what matters is what a visitor receives. They have already caught a share card advertising the wrong product, a homepage whose tier hierarchy had silently inverted, and a hero paragraph sitting 120px out of line with every other element on the site.

images.alt: Terminal output showing the build summary and 42 passing tests
images.caption: Rebuild, then prove it. The build is idempotent — running it twice changes nothing.
